objection: If Jesus is God, why did he pray to God?
answer:
This is exactly the right question to sit with, and I think the "obvious thing" you're missing is simply this: Jesus praying to the Father isn't one mind talking to itself — it's one divine Person, the Son, addressing another divine Person, the Father. God is one being in three distinct persons, and the Son has always been personally distinct from the Father, even before Bethlehem — that's the point of John 17:3, where Jesus prays for the glory he had "with thee before the world was." The Father and the Son were never the same person, so their speaking to one another is real communication between two centers of "I" and "thou," not a soliloquy.

Now add the incarnation: the eternal Son took to himself a genuine human nature, with a human mind, will, and voice that could truly pray, ask, plead, and feel anguish in Gethsemane. So the prayer in the garden isn't evidence he "wasn't really God" or that divinity was something he acquired later — Philippians 2:5–11 is explicit that he already existed in the form of God before he humbled himself and took the form of a servant. The Son didn't stop being God to become man; he added a true humanity to his eternal deity, and it's from within that assumed humanity that he cries "Father, let this cup pass."

That also unlocks "the Father is greater than I" language: as man, in his voluntary humility and submission, the Son is rightly subordinate to the Father in role and mission, even while remaining eternally equal to the Father in nature. A son can be truly equal to his father in being human, while still being under his father's authority — how much more the eternal Son, who submits as man while sharing fully in the Father's Godhead. That's why the same Gospel that records this prayer also opens by calling the Word God and closes with Thomas confessing the risen Jesus as "my Lord and my God" without correction — the Evangelist saw no contradiction, and neither need you.

# Honest Question: Jesus Praying to God

I really do want to understand this, because it's the thing that makes me pause. If Jesus is God, then when he's in the garden at Gethsemane praying, "Father, let this cup pass from me" — isn't he just... talking to himself? That doesn't make sense to me. Or does it mean he *wasn't* really God while he was here on earth, and only became God later? I've read that he said the Father is "greater than I am" — so how can he also be God *and* somehow less than God at the same time? I want to hold onto both the Bible's words *and* the idea that he's God, but right now those feel like they're pulling in opposite directions, and I'm worried I'm missing something obvious.
